title: Cancer Research and Training Coordination
text: The primary goal of the Cancer Center is to promote collaborative interactions across seven consortium institutions that will lead to new approaches to cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. These advances will occur while also advancing the Center’s mission to serve our catchment area and to train future leaders in cancer research.

title: Renovation of Personalized Medicine Facility
text:
The Nutrition and Metabolic Health Center (NMHC) at the University of Louisville will advance 
research on how nutrition and metabolism impact health and chronic diseases such as diabetes, 
obesity, and cardiovascular disorders. By fostering innovative studies, supporting early career 
investigators, and developing cutting-edge research infrastructure, the Center will enhance 
scientific understanding and improve disease prevention and treatment strategies. Through 
collaboration and institutional investment, the NMHC will contribute to better health outcomes in 
Kentucky and beyond by addressing the urgent challenges of poor diet and metabolic dysfunction.

title: Efficient Measurement and Characterization of Genetic Interactions in Cancer Cells
text:
Genetic interactions govern the emergence of phenotype from genotype at every level, but our
capacity to probe and decipher these interactions is severely limited. We propose a hybrid
computational and experimental effort to discover genetic interactions in cancer cells and how
genetic interaction networks are rewired across lineage and oncogenic lesion. Discoveries from
this project will guide combinatorial therapies targeting novel synthetic lethalities and enable
researchers worldwide to gain deeper insight into the complexity of the mammalian cell.

title: PINK1 in the regulation of terminal erythroid maturation and enucleation
text:
The current lack of understanding of mechanisms governing erythroid cell enucleation and overall terminal
erythroid maturation are a major impediment to the advancement of in vitro RBC production from induced
pluripotent stem (iPCSs) and embryonic stem (ES) cells,2 which severely limits our ability to address the current
global blood shortage that plagues several countries.5 Through the completion of the proposed aims, this project
will shed light on PINK1 as a novel regulator of terminal erythroid maturation, and MIRO1 as a mechanistic
regulator of erythroid cell enucleation via PINK1 – which will also have major translational applications.

title: Role of Reelin protein in the cellular and behavioral response to drugs of abuse
text:
Overdose deaths have been on the rise over the past decade, a trend that has been exacerbated by the
current global pandemic, with over 93,000 overdose deaths in 2020. This proposal will investigate cocaine-
dependent signaling related to Reelin, a glycoprotein newly described as a marker of cocaine-responsive
medium spiny neurons. This work will provide novel insight into the molecular basis of substance abuse
disorders that may form the basis of desperately-needed targeted treatment strategies.

title: Chemical Modifications in Regulatory Regions of DNA and RNA
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it helps identify the roles played by
small molecular changes in DNA and RNA bases, often occurring in non-Watson-Crick
structures, that reside in parts of human or viral genomes regulating gene expression. Methods
developed here will aid our ability to sequence genomes, not just for the four common letters A,
C, G and T/U, but also for some of the rare but significant base modifications that impact
mutations, epigenetics, and viral activity.

title: Pediatric Heart Network University of Pittsburgh
text:
This is a collaborative project University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC) Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh
Heart Institute (CHP-HI) to study heart disease in children and young adults with other clinical core research
centers within the NHLBI Pediatric Heart Network. The goal of this project is to develop new knowledge and
understanding that will lead to improved diagnosis and new therapies to lessen the burden of both congenital
and acquired heart disease in a diverse population of children and young adults. CHP-HI is eager to collaborate
with other clinical centers, the data-coordinating center, the NHLBI staff, and industry partners to complete
ongoing studies and initiate innovative new investigations.

title: Extracellular Mitochondria Transfer in Gray and White Matter for Ameliorating Sensorimotor and Cognitive Deficits After Stroke
text:
Project Narrative for R01 application by Hayakawa
 Extracellular mitochondria transfer in gray and white matter for ameliorating sensorimotor and
 cognitive deficits after stroke
 Mitochondria are important for maintaining energy homeostasis in mammalian cells, but it is now
increasingly recognized that mitochondria may be surprisingly release and transfer from cell to cell. Is it
possible that this mitochondrial transfer may represent a novel non-autonomous mechanism to supply energy
and promote neuron-oligodendrocyte-vascular recovery after stroke? Here, we propose that post-translational
modification by O-GlcNAc amplifies extracellular mitochondrial functionality and efficient mitochondrial transfer
that can accelerate the blood-brain barrier repair, remyelination and improve neuroplasticity. Therefore, these
mechanisms should boost sensorimotor recovery and ameliorate post-stroke dementia after focal ischemia.

title: Imaging Biomarker Core G
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – IMAGING BIOMARKER CORE The primary goal of the Imaging Biomarker Core (IBC) is to provide deep phenotyping and longitudinal imaging in all eligible Clinical Core participants representing the heterogeneity of cognitive aging and dementia with A/T/N imaging. Furthermore, the IBC utilizes the latest protocols to collect optimal MRI and PET data, apply state-of- the-art processing pipelines utilizing NU IT’s high-performance computing cluster, and disseminate curated original data or imaging metrics from our pipelines. Prior to the start of the IBC in 2018, approximately 50% of participants had received an MRI, a handful had amyloid, and none had tau imaging. Now, in our actively followed participants, 87% had at least one MRI, 45% had an amyloid scan, and 39% had a tau scan. Additionally, 33% of participants received all three A/T/N scans, thereby providing in-depth characterization. To further improve the quality of imaging, in the next cycle, participants will complete the full suite of A/T/N imaging in two one-hour MR imaging sessions, since the participants need different visits for each PET scan. This also allows us to correct initial quality assurance issues and to collect advanced MR sequences to study underlying vascular and structural physiology. The overall aims of the IBC are: 1) Acquire systematic and multimodal neuroimaging (MR and PET) on all eligible Clinical Core participants without biomarker data or those who have not been imaged in the last 2 years and are of interest for collaborative studies; 2) Curate and distribute integrated imaging datasets and their post-processed metrics to intramural and extramural collaborators, including REC trainee projects, and provide technical support on how to interpret and integrate these measures into their research projects; 3) Incorporate AI and deep learning in data processing and analysis. In addition, the IBC will collaborate with the Administrative, Clinical, Data Management and Statistics, and Neuropathology Cores to expand the analysis of plasma biomarkers for our Clinical Core participants. The IBC will continue to leverage the worldclass imaging facilities of Northwestern for MRI (two 3T Prisma scanners 100% dedicated to research) and PET/CT (three state-of-the-art scanners) in concert with the powerful computing infrastructure provided by Northwestern IT and accessed through our database system NURIPS to provide imaging data and summary metrics to our collaborators. The IBC has strong ties to all the Cores in the Mesulam Institute which enhances all operational and research processes. The IBC places a special emphasis on training and education about neuroimaging methods and analyses to improve the understanding of trainees and junior faculty and allow them to conduct better research.

title: Decoding the Spatial Grammar of Developmental Signaling
text:
A defining goal of regenerative medicine is to build individualized tissues from patient-derived stem cells,
However, current approaches do not offer flexible and precise control over stem cell differentiation in space,
limiting our ability to rationally design tissue structures. Here, we propose a new method that will overcome this
limitation by using spatially-resolved optogenetic stimulation to communicate precise instructions to developing
stem cells.

title: Basic Science Core - Imaging
text: TEXAS BIOMED IN-TRAC Research Imaging Core ABSTRACT The Research Imaging Core will leverage key strengths of Texas Biomed, namely a strong cohort of NIHfunded TB investigators with robust collaboration and experience in different imaging platforms. IN-TRAC participants will benefit from access to unique NHP resources in the Southwest National Primate Research Center (SNPRC) and its cutting edge imaging capabilities. The Research Imaging Core will also establish an education curriculum to introduce IN-TRAC participants to a variety of cell-based and whole animal imaging platforms. AIM 1: Provide didactic and hands-on training program in confocal microscopy and optical imaging. IN-TRAC participants will learn multi-label immunofluorescence or fluorescence in-situ hybridization (FISH) confocal microscopy, which allows for 3- or 4-D evaluation of tissues and cells with multiple fluorochrome labels. AIM 2. Provide didactic and hands-on training in cutting-edge cellular immunology techniques requiring imaging support or computational analysis. The Texas Biomed Biology, Microscopy and Molecular Cores provide high-dimensional, multi-parameter flow cytometry and analysis as well as BSL3 sorting capabilities. Established TB researchers will provide training live cell imaging (Cytation 5) and scRNAseq (10x Genomics) in BSL3. AIM 3: Provide didactic and hands-on training in live imaging using PET/CT and IVIS systems. Training in whole-body live Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) imaging of NHP and in-vivo imaging system (IVIS) of rodents within the BSL3. IN-TRAC participants will extern at the NHP MRI facilities at UTHSCA to learn the advantages and limitations of this imaging platform. At the completion of the Research Imaging Core, participants will be able to effectively interpret published data that use imaging modalities for NHP, rodents, tissues, cells and RNA; design experiments to test their own hypothesis; and participate in TB research that uses the appropriate animal model.

title: Novel approaches to humanized skeletal muscle in pig
text:
This research project seeks a dramatic improvement in the efficiency and production of human skeletal
muscle in pig that will ultimately be used to treat patients with volumetric muscle loss. The overall goal is
to improve the speed, the production and the economic efficiency of pigs with human skeletal muscle at
this critical phase of product development. Achievement of milestones and product development will
provide a platform for the Phase II grant application.

title: UTRGV Center for Genome Research
text: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley seeks to establish a Center for Genome Research that will build genomics research capacity by 1) expanding genomic research capabilities and discoveries in two innovative research projects; and 2) enhancing the size and quality of the available genomics workforce. The Center will leverage the exciting activities and resources available in two highly innovative research projects, one focused on non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and one focused on major depressive disorder. The Center’s structure and approach are designed to expand the pool of genomic scientists, clinician scientists, and researchers at both the doctoral and technical staff levels who can perform cutting-edge multidisciplinary genomics research

title: Macrorecombination in isolated cell pairs via natural genetic transformation
text:
Pathogenic bacteria escape from immune defenses, vaccine protection, and antibiotic therapy by
rapid changes in global gene composition through horizontal gene transfer. This study will develop
tools to observe, for the first time, the complete process of horizontal gene transfer in the major
human pathogen, Streptococcus pneumoniae.

title: Opioid and SUD Data Enclave (O-SUDDEn): Bringing real-time data to the opioid crisis
text: O-SUDDEn will integrate timely real-world data and validated predictive analytics to improve detection of changes in opioid and polysubstance use and forecast overdose-related outcomes. By translating these data into actionable decision-support tools, the project will help state and local agencies deploy evidence-based prevention and treatment resources more effectively and provide a reproducible model for other communities confronting rapidly changing drug environments.

title: The role of Rpl5 haploinsufficiency in hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell function in Diamond Blackfan anemia
text:
The goal of this application is to provide additional training for Sharon Singh MD, a Pediatric
Hematologist/Oncologist, in the evaluation of hematopoiesis by investigating how ribosomal protein
haploinsufficiency alters stem and progenitor cell function. The applicant will be guided by a team of senior
mentors with expertise in stem cell biology, erythropoiesis and anemia with the goal of understanding how
defects in protein synthesis affect red cell biology. There is a critical need for further work in this field, which
has implications for a wide variety of disorders that lead to anemia in children; execution of the proposed aims
will mature the development of a pediatric clinician-scientist with expertise in the evaluation of normal and
abnormal hematopoiesis.

title: Nanomechanical studies of cells and biomolecules
text:
We are developing new nanoscale mechanical techniques and theoretical models to study cells and
biomolecules, and we use these approaches to visualize dynamics of biomolecules in physiologically relevant
conditions and study the physiological role of various forces and mechanical properties in cells. The findings can
help reveal molecular and cellular mechanisms governing biological function and various diseases.

title: Plasmonic Enhanced Raman Structured Illumination Microscopy
text:
Raman scattering microscopy (RSM) is a powerful tool for label-free imaging and the existing
RSM instrument typically has a spatial resolution ~200nm. The proposed research aims to
develop a novel super-resolution RSM technique, i.e. plasmonic enhanced Raman structured
illumination microscopy (PERSIM), and bring the resolution of label-free imaging to the scale of
50 nm. We will construct the PERSIM system in our lab, validate its imaging performance and
compare it with the standard RSM and super-resolution fluoresce imaging.

title: Pathogen Associated Malignancies
text: Nearly 20% of the worldwide burden of cancer is due to pathogens, mostly viruses and some specific bacteria. The Pathogen Associated Malignancies (PAM) Program studies pathogen associated malignancies to better prevent, diagnose, and treat these cancers. Additionally, the program aims to understand the mechanisms by which the microbiome can influence the development of cancers. The program spans basic research, treatment, and public health, and currently has 43 members across three institutions. Program members and leadership have expertise in viral and bacterial pathogenesis, infectious diseases, oncology, and public health research. Basic research focuses on HPV and genetic instability, mechanisms of Merkel Cell polyomavirus oncogenicity, KSHV latency, Helicobacter pylori’s ability to synergize with oncogenic mutations, and the effects of Fusobacterium nucleatum on the tumor microenvironment. Clinical trials include immunotherapeutic approaches to cure Merkel Cell Carcinoma. The program also has human and animal studies exploring the connections between the gut microbiota and cancer outcomes, including graft-versus-host disease, immune reconstitution after hematopoietic cell transplantation, and response to immunotherapy for cancer. The PAM program currently has $12.3M in grant funding (direct costs) of which $4.2M is from NCI. Much of the research is funded by R01s to individual investigators. Large, collaborative grants with members in both PAM and other Consortium programs include a P01 on immunology and immune therapy for Merkel cell carcinoma, a P20 on cancer health disparities, and a U54 on HPV-related cancer prevention. PAM provides many venues to stimulate intra- and inter-programmatic interactions including the yearly retreat bringing together researchers working on the microbiome with those working on virally induced cancers. There are also weekly virology meetings, monthly microbiome meetings and a wide array of sponsored seminars. Pilot grants promote new collaborations between PAM members with other investigators. The program published a total of 330 papers in the current grant cycle, of which 19% were intraprogrammatic and 43% were interprogrammatic.

title: Alcohol-associated cholestatic liver injury and mechanisms
text:
Alcoholic hepatitis (AH) is a severe, potentially life-threatening form of alcohol-associated liver disease
(ALD) with limited therapeutic options. The proposed research focuses on studying the connection
between alcohol-associated cholestasis and AH in a novel murine model for ALD. The proposed
research is expected to lead to an important positive impact on the development of therapeutic strategies
to improve outcomes in patients with AH.
